formationLabel: Early Lithuanian Protestant congregation active before World War I · interdenominational revival in 1951 · ended in 1977
currentUse: The Lithuanian Protestant Parish ended in 1977. Its documented postwar host, St. John the Evangelist Lutheran Church, remains an active LCMS congregation at 195 Maujer Street, Brooklyn, with a current Sunday schedule. The standing host church is a separate institution; its survival does not mean that the Lithuanian parish survives or that St. John holds the Lithuanian parish's records.
summary: New York's Lithuanian Protestant Parish was an interdenominational Lithuanian congregation, not simply a Lutheran or Reformed parish and not St. John the Evangelist Lutheran Church itself. An early congregation operated from the late nineteenth century into the World War I era under ministers including Jonas Drignaitis and Martynas Macaitis. Postwar immigrants revived a Lithuanian Protestant body in 1951 under Rev. Petras Dagys, bringing together Lutheran and Reformed members and some other Christians. Sources conflict between January 21 and October 21 for the founding/revival milestone; a contemporary account and the Mažosios Lietuvos encyclopedia place the first service at St. John on October 21, 1951. The host church is now verified at 195 Maujer Street and remains active, while the Lithuanian parish ended in 1977. No owned building, successor, records-custody transfer, or cemetery has been verified.

historicalNarrative.text: New York's Lithuanian Protestant Parish must be kept interdenominational. The postwar body brought together Lithuanian Lutherans and Reformed Christians and also included some people from other Christian backgrounds; it was not St. John Lutheran Church, a generic Protestant club, or an exclusively Reformed congregation. Mažosios Lietuvos enciklopedija uses several related names for the revived body and identifies Rev. Petras Dagys as its administrator.

historicalNarrative.text: An earlier Lithuanian Protestant congregation operated in New York from the late nineteenth century into the World War I era. The encyclopedia identifies Jonas Drignaitis among its early ministers and Martynas Macaitis from 1914. The reviewed evidence does not provide an incorporation file, exact early worship address, owned building, final early service, or formal dissolution. The later use of revival language therefore supports community lineage but not automatically the same legal corporation.

historicalNarrative.text: Postwar Lithuanian refugees reorganized Protestant congregational life in 1951, but the exact date conflicts. A Dagys biography gives January 21, 1951. The encyclopedia gives October 21 and identifies that date with a service at St. John Evangelical Lutheran Church in Brooklyn; a contemporary 1951 Karys account likewise places Lithuanian Protestant services at St. John on Maujer Street. The dossier retains both readings and treats October 21 as the directly site-linked first-service milestone.

historicalNarrative.text: St. John was a host church rather than the Lithuanian parish's owned property or denominational identity. Its exact current address is 195 Maujer Street. The official LCMS locator and St. John's current website show that the host congregation and building remain active, with present Sunday worship. Those current facts establish the host site's standing condition, but they do not turn St. John into the Lithuanian institution's successor or prove that it holds Lithuanian sacramental and corporate records.

historicalNarrative.text: Mažosios Lietuvos enciklopedija dates the end of the Lithuanian Protestant Parish to 1977. This provides a stronger terminal reading than later directory absence or the death of a pastor, although no closing minutes, corporate dissolution, final-service announcement, merger, or records transfer has been found. The host building survives, while the Lithuanian institution is historical and closed. No separate Lithuanian-owned church, successor congregation, record custodian, or cemetery relationship has been verified.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The 1951 revival date is reported as January 21 in the Dagys biography and October 21 in the encyclopedia; October is tied to the documented St. John first service. The parish was interdenominational and must not be flattened into Lutheran identity based on its host or into Reformed identity based on Dagys. The 1977 institutional end is distinct from the continuing life of the host church. Because no evidence proves that St. John remained the Lithuanian parish's terminal worship site through 1977, the route-level building status is unknown even though the host site's own current condition is standing.
gaps: Early founding date, legal name and incorporation, early sites and addresses, legal continuity into the 1951 revival, exact affiliation agreements, full clergy list, complete postwar worship chronology, final 1977 service, dissolution, successor, records custody, Lithuanian-owned property, and cemetery remain unresolved.
